titre: Diagnostic Performance of Radiomics-Based Machine Learning in Differentiating Glioblastoma From Brain Metastasis: Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
auteurs: Hong C, Liu G, Bie Z, Guo Y, Du Y, Hu Y, Li S, Liu P.
types: meta-analysis systematic review review journal article
resume: Background Glioblastoma (GBM) and brain metastasis (BM) are the most common malignant intracranial tumors in adults. Noninvasive differentiation between them remains challenging, as they frequently share similar imaging features. Although radiomics-based machine learning (ML) models show promise, systematic evidence of their performance remains limited. Objective We aimed to systematically estimate the diagnostic performance of radiomics-based ML models in differentiating GBM from BM and to explore multiclass classification involving primary central nervous system lymphoma (PCNSL), thereby assessing their potential for clinical use. Methods We systematically searched PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, and Cochrane Library databases from inception to January 22, 2026, for studies reporting the diagnostic performance of radiomics-based ML models for differentiating GBM from BM. Multiclass studies involving PCNSL were also retained. Methodological quality was appraised via the Radiomics Quality Score 2.0. Binary diagnostic accuracy was pooled using a bivariate random-effects model, stratified by internal and independent external validation. Multiclass sensitivities and specificities were pooled using separate joint generalized linear mixed models. Physician assessments were evaluated as an exploratory benchmark. Results A total of 39 studies (31 binary and 8 multiclass), involving 11,558 patients, were included. For binary classification, pooled sensitivity and specificity were 88.9% (95% CI 84.1%-92.4%) and 83.0% (95% CI 76.8%-87.9%) in internal validation, and 83.8% (95% CI 77.4%-88.7%) and 80.7% (95% CI 71.1%-87.7%) in external validation, respectively. In multiclass analyses, pooled sensitivity was 84.4% (95% CI 72.4%-91.8%) for GBM, 70.6% (95% CI 54.4%-82.8%) for BM, and 75.0% (95% CI 62.7%-84.3%) for PCNSL, with corresponding specificities of 82.5% (95% CI 70.1%-90.4%), 88.8% (95% CI 81.9%-93.3%), and 94.4% (95% CI 88.4%-97.4%), respectively. Conclusions Radiomics-based ML models could distinguish between GBM and BM in the included cohorts. However, due to methodological limitations and scarce evidence, their generalizability and clinical utility remain unclear. Further multicenter prospective studies should conduct independent external validation in consecutive patients. Trial registration PROSPERO CRD420261295269; https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/view/CRD420261295269.

titre: Image-Based AI for the Diagnosis of Retinopathy of Prematurity: Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
auteurs: Bai H, Zhou Y, Bai Y, Wang Y, Yang Y.
types: meta-analysis systematic review review journal article
resume: Background Retinopathy of prematurity (ROP) is one of the major causes of preventable blindness in premature infants. Early screening, accurate diagnosis, and severity classification are crucial for reducing irreversible visual impairment. Recently, image-based AI models have been widely applied to ROP screening, diagnosis, and severity classification. However, the model architecture, data source, validation method, and diagnostic task vary across studies. Consequently, the overall diagnostic efficiency and clinical utility of deep learning (DL) remain to be systematically assessed. Objective This study aims to evaluate the diagnostic accuracy of image-based AI for ROP by disease type, validation method, model type, and use of transfer learning (TL). Methods We performed a systematic search across Web of Science, Embase, IEEE Xplore, PubMed, and Cochrane Library as of October 12, 2026, to identify studies investigating image-based AI for ROP detection or clinical subtype classification. The risk of bias (RoB) of included studies was assessed using the Quality Assessment of Diagnostic Accuracy Studies 2 (QUADAS-2) tool. Sensitivity and specificity were pooled using bivariate mixed-effects models, with analyses stratified by diagnostic task and validation method. Results Sixty-two studies contributed 185 contingency tables. For normal vs ROP, pooled sensitivity was 0.94 (95% CI 0.92-0.96) and specificity was 0.96 (95% CI 0.94-0.97). For normal vs treatment-requiring ROP (TR-ROP), sensitivity was 0.97 (95% CI 0.91-0.99) and specificity was 0.74 (95% CI 0.66-0.80). For mild vs severe ROP, specificity was 0.78 (95% CI 0.59-0.90). In external validation, pooled sensitivity and specificity were 0.95 (95% CI 0.89-0.97) and 0.83 (95% CI 0.72-0.90), respectively, while the corresponding estimates were 0.95 (95% CI 0.93-0.96) and 0.97 (95% CI 0.96-0.98) in internal validation. For DL and conventional machine learning (ML) models, pooled sensitivity was 0.95 (95% CI 0.94-0.96) and 0.96 (95% CI 0.90-0.98), respectively, while specificity was 0.96 (95% CI 0.95-0.97) and 0.91 (95% CI 0.84-0.94), respectively. With and without TL, pooled sensitivity was 0.95 (95% CI 0.94-0.96) and 0.95 (95% CI 0.92-0.97), respectively, while specificity was 0.97 (95% CI 0.96-0.98) and 0.92 (95% CI 0.86-0.95), respectively. Conclusions Image-based AI may have high sensitivity for ROP assessment, but its specificity is lower for identifying TR-ROP and in the external-validation subgroup. Given the predominance of retrospective studies, heterogeneity, and limited external validation, current evidence supports AI as an adjunct to screening and referral, with clinicians retaining responsibility for diagnostic and treatment decisions. Prospective, multicenter external validation is needed. Trial registration PROSPERO CRD420261418502; https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/view/CRD420261418502.

titre: MRI-based radiomics and deep learning for the prenatal diagnosis of Placenta Accreta Spectrum: a systematic review and exploratory meta-analysis.
auteurs: Sirico A, Pisani D, Sandullo L, Fatigati M, Mappa I, Maruotti GM, Rizzo G, Cobellis L.
resume: Objective accuracy of Placenta Accreta Spectrum (PAS) diagnosis using conventional magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is still limited by subjective interpretation. Increasing evidence showed that radiomics and Deep Learning (DL) may improve diagnostic objectivity by extracting quantitative features from MRI data. This study aimed to synthesize the evidence on the diagnostic performance and clinical utility of these models. Methods a systematic review and meta-analysis was conducted following PRISMA-DTA guidelines and PRISMA 2020 recommendations: PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science databases from inception to December 2025. We searched for primary studies evaluating MRI-based radiomics or DL models for the binary diagnosis of PAS. Data were extracted to create 2 × 2 contingency tables and used a bivariate random-effects model to calculate pooled sensitivity, specificity, and to generate a summary ROC (SROC) curve. We assessed robustness via leave-one-out sensitivity analysis, and clinical utility using Fagan's nomogram and likelihood ratios. A secondary meta-analysis was performed for the prediction of postpartum hemorrhage (PPH) ≥1000 mL. Results twelve studies met the inclusion criteria (N = 1135 patients). The pooled sensitivity for PAS diagnosis was 0.83 (95% CI: 0.75-0.89) and pooled specificity was 0.82 (95% CI: 0.74-0.88). The summary AUC was 0.896, confirming high diagnostic accuracy. The positive likelihood ratio (LR+) was 4.61 and the negative likelihood ratio (LR-) was 0.21. Subgroup analyses based on AI model type (p > 0.05) and study design (p > 0.05) did not find significant differences between groups but revealed that single-center studies tended to report higher accuracy compared to multicenter studies. The secondary meta-analysis on massive PPH prediction (n = 4 studies, N = 353 patients: 165 PPH+ and 188 PPH-) yielded a pooled sensitivity of 0.88 (95% CI: 0.63-0.97), a pooled specificity of 0.78 (95% CI: 0.50-0.93), and an AUC of 0.901. Conclusions MRI-based AI models demonstrate high exploratory pooled accuracy for the prenatal diagnosis of PAS in high-risk cohorts. These results suggest that these tools show promising exploratory accuracy and may provide decision support as an adjunct ("human-in-the-loop") in equivocal cases. However, their real-world clinical generalizability remains constrained by retrospective designs and index test threshold optimization.

titre: Use of Large Language Models for Structured Quantitative and Qualitative Analysis of Simulation Debriefings Using the DASH Framework (AIDE Study): Prospective Observational Study.
auteurs: Pico J, Bouhadiba T, Jazestani S, Zhu E, Nguyen BK, Baroudi R, Dababneh S, Tanoubi I.
resume: Background Simulation-based education is a cornerstone of health care training, with debriefing representing the critical phase of a learning process. However, assessing debriefing quality remains challenging, relying largely on expert judgment and structured tools such as the Debriefing Assessment for Simulation in Healthcare (DASH). The emergence of AI, particularly large language models (LLMs), offers new opportunities for the automated analysis of educational interactions. Objective This study aimed to explore the feasibility and characteristics of AI-automated analysis of postsimulation debriefings using the DASH framework. Methods We conducted a prospective, single-center, observational study at the Centre d'Apprentissage des Attitudes et Habiletés Cliniques ( Université de Montréal ). Postsimulation debriefings involving anesthesia residents in postgraduate years 2 and 4 were conducted by a single instructor, audio-recorded, transcribed, and anonymized. Transcripts were analyzed using a natural language processing model (ChatGPT) with a structured prompt aligned with the 6 DASH elements. For each debriefing, the model generated a structured qualitative evaluation, including a rating for each DASH element using the original 7-point DASH effectiveness scale and an identification of strengths and areas for improvement, supported by transcript excerpts. No comparison with a human DASH-trained evaluator was performed. Results A total of 30 debriefings were included, with no exclusions or technical issues. A complete, structured AI-generated evaluation across all 6 DASH elements was obtained for all 30 (100%) debriefings, meeting the predefined feasibility outcome. "Establishes an engaging learning environment," "Maintains an engaging learning environment," "Provokes engaging discussion," and "Identifies and explores performance gaps" each had a median rating of 6 (IQR 6-7, 6-6, 6-7, and 6-6, respectively). "Structures the debriefing in an organized way" had the lowest median rating, at 4 (IQR 4-5), while "Helps trainees achieve or sustain good future performance" had a median rating of 5 (IQR 5-6). A cross-debriefing analysis identified recurring patterns across sessions, including consistent learner engagement and opportunities to improve debriefing structure and the formulation of strategies to support future performance. Conclusions This study demonstrates the feasibility of AI-assisted qualitative assessment of postsimulation debriefings using an LLM prompted in accordance with the DASH framework. AI may represent a complementary tool to support pedagogical analysis, instructor reflection, and faculty development in simulation-based education. Although this exploratory study focused on textual transcript analysis without incorporating nonverbal communication or expert benchmarking, the findings support the feasibility of AI-assisted debriefing assessment and provide a foundation for future validation studies. Further research comparing AI-generated and expert evaluations could help refine these approaches and inform their integration into simulation-based education and faculty development.

titre: Blood Pressure Estimation for Hemodynamic Monitoring Using Reduced Photoplethysmography Features in Intensive Care Units: Prospective Machine Learning Study.
auteurs: Lee J, Sujanyal SA, Dadwal S, Omercikoglu E, Alazab HM, Handral MS, Shariff MN, Nechooli MA, Chandrasekar S, Shivaram S, C M V, Arunachalam SP, Helgeson SA.
resume: Background Continuous, noninvasive blood pressure (BP) monitoring is clinically important for managing hemodynamic instability in the intensive care unit (ICU). However, current ICU practice primarily relies on invasive arterial catheterization. While this is the clinical gold standard for continuous measurement, it carries risks such as infection and thrombosis and is typically limited to select critical care settings. Objective To reduce reliance on invasive arterial lines, we developed an interpretable estimation framework for systolic blood pressure (SBP), mean arterial pressure (MAP), and diastolic blood pressure (DBP) from single-sensor photoplethysmography (PPG). Methods Synchronized PPG and arterial line 10-minute recordings from 100 patients in the ICU were analyzed. Using a hybrid feature selection strategy (RReliefF and intrinsic model-specific rankings), we reduced 201 initial features to an optimized subset of 30 core features. Model development and evaluation were designed to minimize information leakage and overfitting, incorporating nested cross-validation and patient-wise testing to assess generalizability across heterogeneous ICU populations. We developed and validated predictive models using machine learning techniques, specifically XGBoost (XGB), random forest, and support vector regression, with XGB serving as our primary model. Results Among the evaluated models, the Hybrid Top 30 XGB configuration provided the best balance between estimation performance, model compactness, and computational efficiency. The model achieved mean absolute errors of 8.61 mm Hg (SBP), 3.50 mm Hg (MAP), and 2.62 mm Hg (DBP). For MAP and DBP, mean difference (SD) values of -0.09 (4.54) mm Hg and -1.07 (3.51) mm Hg, respectively, satisfied the Association for the Advancement of Medical Instrumentation numerical criteria, while performance corresponded to Grade A according to the British Hypertension Society grading criteria. Although SBP exhibited greater variability, estimation performance was largely preserved using a physiologically informed subset of 30 features (approximately 15% of the original feature set). Feature importance analysis revealed distinct physiological feature patterns across SBP, MAP, and DBP estimation. Conclusions Interpretability analysis identified key predictors associated with wave reflection, systolic timing, low-frequency vasomotor activity, and autonomic regulation. By explicitly linking predictive features to underlying cardiovascular physiology, the proposed framework addresses a key limitation of existing black-box cuffless BP models. Ultimately, this study demonstrates that an optimized XGB framework using physiologically informed PPG features can provide accurate and computationally efficient BP estimation in ICU settings and may support the assessment of clinically relevant hemodynamic states using a single-sensor PPG platform. These findings provide a foundation for future development of more robust and generalizable interpretable BP estimation models and cuffless monitoring technologies.

titre: Bias and equity in large language model-based applications for health care: a scoping review.
auteurs: Liao J, Li H, Yang R, Nair SV, Zhu W, Liew JCK, Zhang P, Liu M, Ning Y, Elangovan K, Ke Y, Hong C, Ong JCL, Chen Q, Alsentzer E, Bitterman DS, Ting DSW, Liu N.
resume: The integration of large language models (LLMs) into health care presents both opportunities for innovation and risks of perpetuating existing biases and health disparities. Although these concerns are widely discussed, a systematic understanding of the research landscape regarding bias and equity in LLM-based applications for health care remains limited, and few discussions have translated into actionable mitigation strategies. We conducted a Scoping Review to systematically map this landscape and identify key trends and gaps. We searched PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, and Scopus for English-language articles published from Jan 1, 2018, to March 10, 2026. Our analysis of the 201 included studies revealed a strong focus on specific medical contexts and demographic factors and a predominant reliance on proprietary models that constrain transparency in bias evaluation. A disconnect exists between bias detection and mitigation, and the potential of LLMs to promote health equity remains underexplored. To realise a more coherent integration of bias mitigation and health equity objectives in health-care LLM development, the field needs large-scale, endpoint-driven studies grounded in real-world clinical workflows. Furthermore, we advocate for standardised multidimensional bias evaluation frameworks developed with support from professional societies and lifecycle bias governance across both proprietary and open-weight models to guide the safe and equitable integration of LLMs into health care globally.
